title: Listening practice: A fraction problem, a past event and a writing lesson
description: Three recordings: students explain a muffin problem, a narrator describes a fire from the past, and a teacher explains summary writing.

stimuli.title: Listen: A problem about a bake sale

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: Here's a problem about a school bake sale. The club baked five trays of muffins, and each tray holds twelve muffins. They sold three fourths of all the muffins before noon. Rafael thinks they have fifteen muffins left. Ana, do you agree?

turns.speaker: Ana
turns.text: Yes, I agree with Rafael. First, I found the total: five times twelve is sixty muffins. Then, since they sold three fourths, one fourth is left. One fourth of sixty is fifteen. I also checked it another way: three fourths of sixty is forty-five, and sixty minus forty-five is fifteen.

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: Nice work. Dev, what would change if each tray held sixteen muffins?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Then the total would be eighty, and one fourth of eighty is twenty. So they'd have twenty left.

stimuli.title: Listen: An event from the past

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Let me take you back to London. It was September, sixteen sixty-six, when a small fire began in a bakery on Pudding Lane. Imagine the city then: most houses were made of wood and built very close together, and the summer had been long and dry. Then a strong wind carried sparks from roof to roof, so the fire spread quickly. For about four days, flames moved through the city. Many people grabbed what they could and ran to boats on the river or to open fields outside the walls. Finally, the wind weakened, and workers pulled down buildings to make gaps. Then the fire stopped. Thousands of homes had been destroyed. Afterward, the city made new rules: new houses had to be built with brick or stone, and streets were made wider. Over time, London was rebuilt as a safer city.

stimuli.title: Listen: A writing workshop

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: Before we start our summaries today, I want to explain our routine. We write silently for ten minutes before we share with partners. Why? Because if you hear your partner's ideas first, you might drop your own. Quiet time gives every writer a chance to think independently. Now, a good summary includes the main idea and the most important details, in your own words. It does not include your opinion. For example, if you write "I think this article is boring," that's an opinion, so it doesn't belong. Finally, look at how small connecting words change a sentence. Suppose I write: "The town planted trees; however, many of them died." The word "however" tells the reader that the second idea is a problem or a surprise, so the sentence feels different than if I had written "and." Pay attention to those small words when you revise.

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Can we use "however" in our summaries?

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: Yes, whenever the two ideas truly contrast.

items.stem: How many muffins did the club bake in all?

options.text: 17 muffins
45 muffins
60 muffins
15 muffins

distractors.a: That is five plus twelve; the club baked five trays with twelve on each, so the total comes from multiplying.
distractors.b: Forty-five is the number sold, not the total.
distractors.d: Fifteen is the number left, not the total.

items.explanation: The club baked five trays with twelve muffins on each tray, and Ana says five times twelve is sixty muffins.

support.clue: Listen to the teacher's first sentences and to Ana's first calculation. She uses the number of trays and the number on each tray.
support.frame: The club baked ______ trays with ______ muffins on each tray, so there were ______ in all.
support.model: Mentor example. "The school ordered four boxes with nine pencils in each box, so there were thirty-six pencils in all." Multiply to find a total. Find the total number of muffins the same way.

items.stem: How does Ana check her answer?

options.text: She finds three fourths, then subtracts.
She counts the muffins on each tray.
She asks Rafael to count the leftovers.
She divides the total by three, then adds.

distractors.b: Ana multiplies to find the total; she does not count tray by tray.
distractors.c: Rafael is mentioned only because he has the same answer.
distractors.d: Ana does not divide by three. She finds three fourths of the total and subtracts it from the total.

items.explanation: Ana says three fourths of sixty is forty-five, and sixty minus forty-five is fifteen, which matches her first answer.

support.clue: Listen to the end of Ana's turn. She says I also checked it another way.
support.frame: Ana checks her answer a second way: first she finds ______, then she ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "To check 24 ÷ 4 = 6, I multiply 6 × 4 and get 24 again." A check uses a second method to see if the result matches. Listen for Ana's second method.

misconceptions.b: mixes up finding the total with checking
misconceptions.d: reads three fourths as dividing by three

items.stem: Each tray now holds sixteen muffins. What does Dev conclude, and why?

options.text: Fifteen are left, because the fraction sold is the same.
Twenty are left, because one fourth of eighty is twenty.
Sixty are left, because three fourths of eighty is sixty.
Sixteen are left, because each tray holds sixteen.

distractors.a: The total changes to eighty, so one fourth is no longer fifteen.
distractors.c: Sixty is the number sold, not the number left.
distractors.d: The tray size is not the number of muffins left.

items.explanation: Dev says the total would be eighty, and one fourth of eighty is twenty, so twenty muffins would be left.

support.clue: Listen to Dev's whole turn. The tray size changes, so the total changes. Ask yourself: is the answer the amount sold or the amount left?
support.frame: Dev says ______ are left, because one fourth of ______ is ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "If the box holds 20 crayons and one fifth are broken, then 4 are broken, because one fifth of 20 is 4." A conclusion names the amount and gives a reason. Say Dev's conclusion the same way.

misconceptions.d: mixes up tray size and total

items.stem: Put the events in the order the narrator tells them.

items.text: Workers pulled down buildings to make gaps
A fire started in a bakery
The city made new building rules
People carried their belongings to boats
Wind carried sparks from roof to roof

items.explanation: The fire started in a bakery, wind carried sparks, people ran to boats and fields, workers pulled down buildings to stop it, and afterward the city made new rules.

support.clue: Listen for the time words: September, then, for about four days, finally, and afterward.
support.frame: First, ______. Then ______. Next, ______. After that, ______. Afterward, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "First, a storm knocked down a tree. Then neighbors cut it into pieces. Next, a truck hauled it away. Afterward, the town planted a new tree." Time words show the order. Order the events in the audio the same way.

facts: The Great Fire of London began in September 1666 in a bakery on Pudding Lane.
Most London houses were wooden and close together.
After the fire, new rules required brick or stone houses and wider streets.

items.stem: Why did the fire spread so quickly?

options.text: People carried their belongings to boats on the river.
Wooden houses stood close, and wind carried sparks.
The new rules allowed houses to be made of wood.
Workers pulled down buildings near the bakery.

distractors.a: People moved their belongings to boats to escape; that did not spread the fire.
distractors.c: The new rules came afterward, and they required brick or stone.
distractors.d: Pulling down buildings made gaps that helped stop the fire.

items.explanation: The narrator says houses were made of wood and built close together, and a strong wind carried sparks from roof to roof, so the fire spread quickly.

support.clue: Listen to the second and third sentences. Notice the word so.
support.model: Mentor example. "The pond dried up because the summer was hot and no rain fell for weeks." A cause can have more than one part. Find the causes the narrator gives.

facts: The Great Fire of London spread quickly because the houses were wooden and close together and a strong wind carried sparks.

misconceptions.c: mixes up the order of events

items.stem: Why does the teacher have students write silently before sharing?

options.text: So partners can check spelling first.
So the teacher can read summaries first.
So partners can share ideas before writing.
So writers don't drop their own ideas.

distractors.b: The teacher says nothing about reading summaries first.
distractors.c: The teacher says partners share after the silent writing.

items.explanation: The teacher says that if students hear a partner's ideas first, they might drop their own, so quiet time lets every writer think independently.

support.clue: Listen for the question Why? and the word Because right after it.
support.frame: The teacher has students write silently so that ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "We stretch before dance class so that our muscles are ready." A purpose often follows the words so that. Find the teacher's purpose.

items.stem: Which two things does the teacher say about the writing routine?

options.text: Writers write silently for ten minutes.
Writers write silently for fifteen minutes.
Writers share with partners after the quiet time.
Writers share with partners before the quiet time.

distractors.b: The teacher says ten minutes, not fifteen.
distractors.d: The teacher says writers share with partners after the quiet time, not before.

items.explanation: The teacher says students write silently for ten minutes before they share with partners.

support.clue: Listen to the second and third sentences of the talk. Listen for the number of minutes and for what happens first.
support.frame: Writers write silently for ______ minutes before they ______.
support.model: Mentor example. 'In our band, we warm up for five minutes before we play the song.' A speaker can say how long something lasts and what comes first. Listen for both in the teacher's routine.

items.stem: What does the word "however" do in the teacher's example sentence?

options.text: It shows the second idea is a problem or a surprise.
It shows the second idea adds one more good thing.
It shows the second idea happened before the first.
It shows the writer is asking a question.

distractors.b: The teacher says however shows a problem or a surprise, not one more good thing. That is what "and" would do.
distractors.c: However signals a contrast, not a time order.
distractors.d: The teacher's example is still a statement.

items.explanation: The teacher says the word however tells the reader that the second idea is a problem or a surprise.

support.clue: Listen to the teacher's explanation right after the example sentence about trees.
support.frame: The word "however" shows that the second idea is ______ the first idea.
support.model: Mentor example. "I studied all night; nevertheless, the test felt hard." A connecting word tells the reader how two ideas relate. Say how "however" relates the two ideas in the teacher's sentence.

misconceptions.d: confuses a connecting word with punctuation
